European healthcare stocks have solidified their safe-haven status amid doubts about AI
sum: Steady profit growth and demand for key drugs are making the European healthcare sector a safe haven from the volatility of AI companies' stocks, according to Bloomberg
European healthcare companies have exceeded forecasts for the 11th consecutive quarter / Photo: Mahir Asadli / Shutterstock

Against the backdrop of growing uncertainty surrounding investments in artificial intelligence, the “defensive appeal” of European healthcare stocks is on the rise, Bloomberg noted. In the third quarter, companies in this sector posted their strongest earnings growth in two years, the agency notes, emphasizing that their actual results have exceeded expectations for 11 consecutive quarters. As a result, these companies’ earnings per share are also rising, Bloomberg observes.

Earnings per share for companies in the MSCI Europe Health Care Index (which tracks the performance of large- and mid-cap companies in the healthcare sector across 15 developed European countries, including shares of Roche, Novartis, AstraZeneca, Novo Nordisk, GSK, Sanofi) rose 13% in the third quarter—the fastest pace for that period in the last two years—while analysts had expected growth of only 2.4%, according to Bloomberg. More than 71% of companies in the sector exceeded earnings forecasts.

Moreover, the growth was widespread: pharmaceutical companies’ revenue in the third quarter rose 8.4% compared with an expected 7%, while profits for medical equipment manufacturers and healthcare service providers increased by 11% against a forecast of 4.1%, according to data from Bloomberg Intelligence (BI). AstraZeneca’s profits exceeded analysts’ estimates thanks to strong growth in its oncology division, while high demand for biosimilars and services at its hospitals helped Germany’s Fresenius beat expectations. Companies with a significant share of sales in the U.S. also benefited from the strengthening dollar, Bloomberg reports.

France's Sanofi, which generates about half of its revenue in the U.S., has raised its sales and profit forecasts twice amid growing demand for Dupixent, its best-selling drug for treating skin conditions and asthma.

Shares in Glanbia tumble amid Kirkland concerns
sum: Shareholders in Glanbia saw the value of the company’s stock drop by more than 11% between the close on Friday 20 November and the end of trading on Tuesday 24 November.

The rapid reversal in fortunes for the company is being blamed on the risk from increased competition in the key US market. Specifically, the worries surround retailer Costco’s move to restock its own-brand protein powder under its premium Kirkland label.

The Kirkland brand is listed at $64.99 (€59.25) while Glanbia’s Optimum Nutrition retails at $89.99 (€82.06) in Costco. The Glanbia package has more servings than the Kirkland brand, so the price differential per serving is significantly smaller than the price per pack.

The biggest risk for Glanbia is that it will lose shelf-space in Costco. When the retailer first launched its Kirkland protein powder in the US in 2025, it led to a drop in shelf space for Optimum Nutrition. There is no evidence yet that this has happened with the relaunch. According to Costco stock tracking website Warehouse Runner, the Kirkland brand is currently available in around 40% of Costco’s more than 650 stores in the US, while Optimum Nutrition is available in almost every location.
That being said, the extra competition from a discounter’s own brand in the critically important US market appears to have made shareholders nervous about Glanbia’s growth outlook.

In the first week of November, Glanbia upgraded its earnings per share growth forecast to between 22% and 24% for 2026. Speaking at the time, CEO Hugh McGuire said that the long-term fundamental demand for whey remains strong.

An analyst note from stockbroker Goodbody’s head of consumer research Patrick Higgins, published on Monday, suggested that the company shares had sold off too much in reaction to the Costco news. “We consider the pull-back to be considerably overdone at these levels,” he wrote.

items.t: Roche's Oral Breast Cancer Drug Wilserdly Wins Dual FDA Approvals; CEO Sees It Vying for Best-Selling Drug in History
sum: Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche said Tuesday that its newly approved oral breast cancer drug Wilserdly (generic name giredestrant) has the potential to surpass Ocrevus, currently its best-selling multiple sclerosis treatment, and become the company's top-selling product since its founding. The remarks came after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Monday broadened the drug's approved uses.

The FDA approved Wilserdly as a monotherapy for adjuvant treatment of adult patients with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative breast cancer at intermediate-to-high risk of recurrence in stages I through III. Market sources noted this marks the first new hormonal therapy option for this particular type of early-stage breast cancer in more than two decades.

Wilserdly is a next-generation oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) with full antagonist activity. Its mechanism of action blocks estrogen from binding to the receptor and promotes degradation of the estrogen receptor protein, thereby suppressing cancer cell proliferation. Roche said the breast cancer subtype targeted by the drug accounts for roughly 70% of all breast cancer cases, all sharing the characteristic that estrogen fuels cancer cell growth.

Clinical trial data showed that Wilserdly reduced the risk of breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared with existing therapies. With the early-stage adjuvant indication cleared, the drug's reach has extended from advanced disease to early-stage adjuvant treatment, covering patients across different stages of the disease.

In fact, the FDA had already approved Wilserdly in combination with everolimus on November 16 for previously treated patients with ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer. That made Wilserdly the fourth oral SERD drug approved for the market.

Teresa Graham, CEO of Roche's pharmaceuticals division, described the approval on a conference call with reporters as marking a "new era" in breast cancer treatment, saying flatly that "we believe Wilserdly has the potential to be Roche's best-selling medicine." She did not provide specific sales forecasts but said she expects Wilserdly's peak sales to be comparable to those of Ocrevus.

BioNTech Rewrites Its Roche Pact and Buys an FDA Fast Lane While Tightening 2026 Guidance
sum: BioNTech has been working two timelines at once: the revenue it books this year and the regulatory runway for a cancer drug still in late-stage development. The Mainz-based biotech moved on both fronts in recent weeks, striking a $205 million deal for an FDA priority review voucher and restructuring its cost-sharing arrangement with Roche and Genentech — a switch to a royalty model that takes effect January 1, 2027, at which point the two partners will generally shoulder the program's future research and development costs.

The voucher purchase, agreed with Scholar Rock, hands BioNTech an expedited FDA review ticket it intends to attach to a future marketing application from its advanced oncology pipeline. Cash consideration is set at $205 million, and the transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including antitrust clearance under the Hart-Scott-Rodino process.

The company's third-quarter 2026 report, released in early November, showed revenue of EUR 1.29 billion and net profit of EUR 184.5 million. Alongside those figures, BioNTech refined its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to the upper end of its prior range, now projecting EUR 1.7 billion to EUR 1.9 billion. Cash, cash equivalents and securities investments stood at EUR 16.2 billion at the close of the quarter.

Analysts have been adjusting their models in response. Citi's Geoff Meacham reaffirmed his rating on November 11. At J.P. Morgan, Jessica Fye kept a "Neutral" stance on Thursday while nudging her price target to $93 from $92.
Shares slipped 0.5% in the prior session, closing at EUR 73.80.

The transaction, which remains subject to customary conditions including US antitrust clearance, buys the company a faster track through the Food and Drug Administration's review process.

The voucher purchase sits alongside a separate move to lighten BioNTech's research burden. The company has exercised an option in its collaboration with Roche and Genentech under which the two partners will, from January 1, 2027, generally shoulder future research and development costs for the program in question. The ongoing adjuvant pancreatic cancer study is to continue as planned.

Beyond the Lab: What Students Can Learn From the Future Forward: A Roche-Genentech Early Career Expedition Event
sum: As AI undoubtedly seeps into every aspect of our lives, hiring processes and career exploration is one of the most impacted sectors, what does it take to stand out in biotech & life science recruiting?

With most major companies switching their hiring process to be AI automated—from resume scanners to online AI interviews—it can be difficult to break into the daunting world of biotech. For students interested in breaking into life sciences and biotech, breaking through the ‘AI wall’ is a challenge, especially when scanners specifically look for relevant experience. I joined a day-long virtual career exploration event hosted by Roche/Genentech where managers and recruiters share their perspective about early career hiring.
I. A Resume May Get Your Foot in the Door, But Experience Tells the Story

Having a perfectly tailored resume is becoming easier and easier with AI tools that can take a job description and edit an application/resume accordingly. However, having the perfect resume does not make someone the perfect candidate. During the event, Shannon Noonan—Principle Staffing Consultant and Talent Acquisition & Strategy @ Genentech—and Jennifer Moore—Senior Principle Technical Manager @ Genentech—discussed their perspectives about the modern day hiring process. They emphasized that recruiters look for experiences and relevant work that is specific to their project, not just the most impressive resume or most experiences. So, rejection doesn’t mean a candidate isn’t “good enough,” it just means the hiring manager is looking for skills that apply to their specific projects. Instead of submitting the same resume to every position, taking the time to understand what the role entails and tailoring your resume accordingly can be extremely beneficial. However, if a manager is hiring for a biotech marketing position, those with technical skills or lab experience will not be best suited for the role. Another point that they emphasized was being able to effectively communicate every role on your resume.
II. Interviews Aren’t Performances; They Should be Interactive Conversations
Preparing for an interview can often feel like memorizing a script for every possible question. But, interviews shouldn’t feel rehearsed, according to Genentech hiring managers.

Faeth Therapeutics signs Roche supply deal for breast cancer trial
sum: A Phase 1b/2 breast-cancer study will test PIKTOR with the experimental hormone therapy giredestrant after Faeth Therapeutics, Inc. NASDAQFTH announced a clinical collaboration on Monday. Interim data from the breast-cancer trial are expected in 2027.
Faeth will sponsor and conduct study FTH-PIK-101 under the agreement with F. Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd. Roche SWXRO SWXROP OTCMKTSRHHBY will supply giredestrant, while Faeth retains all rights to PIKTOR.
Faeth is an Austin-based clinical-stage biotechnology company built around its lead oral cancer regimen, with development programmes in breast and endometrial cancer.
Shares last closed at US$10.03 on Nasdaq at 4:00 p.m. EST on Nov. 13, according to Google Finance NASDAQFTH. That close precedes Monday's announcement and does not measure investors' response.

The disclosed obligations leave study sponsorship and conduct with Faeth and drug supply with Roche. The Nov. 16 announcement does not disclose an upfront payment, milestone schedule or cost-sharing formula. It provides no financial terms with which to quantify Roche's development exposure beyond supplying medicine.

The study targets hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. Faeth says activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway is a recognised mechanism of resistance to endocrine therapy, providing the rationale for combining PIKTOR with a hormone-directed treatment.

PIKTOR combines serabelisib, a PI3K-alpha inhibitor, with sapanisertib, an mTORC1/mTORC2 inhibitor. The approach is designed to block several points in the same pathway; its proposed benefit alongside giredestrant remains to be established in patients.

sum: Halozyme Therapeutics HALO has collaboration agreements with large pharma companies, which use its ENHANZE technology for the development of subcutaneous (SC) formulations of their various approved drugs. The company has several marketed partnered drugs based on this technology, including the subcutaneous formulation of J&J’s JNJ Darzalex, argenx’s ARGX Vyvgart Hytrulo as well as Roche’s RHHBY Phesgo.

Per the agreements, these companies have been granted worldwide license rights to develop and commercialize their products using ENHANZE technology. These deals generate royalties on sales of marketed drugs, milestone payments and annual license fees, which comprise Halozyme’s top line.

For the first nine months of 2026, Halozyme's total revenues rose 43% year over year to $1.35 billion. Royalty revenues rose 45.8% to $889.4 million, driven by higher royalties from J&J for SC Darzalex, argenx for Vyvgart Hytrulo and Roche for Phesgo. Royalties accounted for approximately 66% of the company’s total revenues during this period.
Reflecting the strength of its overall business performance, Halozyme raised its total revenue guidance for 2026 last week when it reported better-than-expected third-quarter 2026 results.

The company raised its total revenue guidance to $1.86-$1.925 billion, indicating growth of 33-38%. HALO also raised its royalty revenue guidance to $1.24-$1.26 billion from the previous range of $1.22-$1.24 billion. The updated outlook implies year-over-year growth of 42-45%.

We expect Halozyme to sustain strong revenue growth through the remainder of 2026, driven by rising royalty contributions from its partnered drugs. Continued sales growth of established ENHANZE-enabled products is expected to support the company's royalty stream.

Global Alzheimer’s trial summit to unveil AriBio phase 3 pill data and next-wave therapies
sum: An international conference that will showcase the latest progress in developing treatments for Alzheimer's disease—the leading cause of dementia—will be held in the United States next week. Results will include the global phase 3 trial of an oral Alzheimer's drug under development by Korean biotech AriBio, along with next-generation candidates that target brain inflammation and tau protein.

The meeting will also focus on real-world experience with existing Alzheimer's drugs and early-diagnosis technologies that use blood tests and other tools. The field is seen as expanding beyond amyloid-clearing approaches to a wider set of therapeutic targets.

The 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference (CTAD 2026) will take place in Boston from the 16th to the 19th (local time). CTAD, held annually since 2008, is a global meeting dedicated to clinical research in Alzheimer's, where researchers and drugmakers from around the world present new drug development and trial results.

Ahead of the event, the organizing committee highlighted as key readouts this year: ▲ the global phase 3 study of AriBio's 'AR1001,' ▲ a phase 2a trial of 'NTRX-07,' which targets neuroinflammation and is being developed by U.S. biotech NeuroTherapia, and ▲ a phase 2b study of 'PRI-002,' an early Alzheimer's candidate from German biotech Priavoid GmbH.

Korean biotech AriBio will present results from the global phase 3 'POLARIS-AD' study of AR1001 on the opening day, the 16th. Sharon Sha, a professor at Stanford University School of Medicine and the global principal investigator, will deliver the presentation.

AR1001 is an oral, once-daily Alzheimer's drug candidate. It is being developed to inhibit PDE5—an enzyme involved in signaling between neurons in the brain—to improve neuronal function and slow disease progression.
The phase 3 trial enrolled 1,535 patients with early Alzheimer's. Patients received AR1001 or placebo for 52 weeks, and researchers assessed changes in cognition and activities of daily living.

StockWatch: Nurix Nosedives as Sanofi Halts Phase I Immunology Candidate
sum: Nurix Therapeutics (Nasdaq: NRIX) suffered its worst one-day loss as a public company Wednesday when Sanofi (Euronext Paris: SAN and Nasdaq: SNY) terminated development of the Phase I immunology candidate SAR448272 (NX-3911)—a key program of the companies’ nearly seven-year, up to $ 2.5 billion collaboration to discover, develop, and commercialize protein degradation drugs for “challenging” diseases.

The rest of the collaboration continues despite Sanofi pulling the plug on SAR448272 (NX-3911), an oral signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6) degrader that had been under study in a Phase I first-in-human trial in Europe (European Union Clinical Trials Register number 2026-526014-87-00). The trial began recruiting patients in Germany in July and had planned to expand recruitment into the Czech Republic, France, Italy, and Spain, a milestone that triggered a $10 million payment from Sanofi to Nurix in August.

STAT6, a key drug target in type 2 inflammation, is among the five targets identified by the companies in their collaboration, which took effect in January 2020 when Sanofi paid Nurix $55 million upfront. At the time, Sanofi committed to paying Nurix up to $2.5 billion in total payments, most of that tied to achieving research, preclinical, clinical, regulatory, and sales milestones.

As of August 31, Sanofi had paid Nurix a total $129 million—the $55 million upfront; $22 million in 2021 when Sanofi exercised an option to expand from three to five targets; $22 million for achieving research milestones; and $30 million for license extension fees—according to Nurix’s Form 10-Q quarterly report for the third quarter, filed October 13.

Nurix insisted that its recent cash runway guidance would not be affected by Sanofi’s halting development of SAR448272. Nurix said it had enough cash to fund operations into the second half of 2029 based on its $1.1 billion of cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities as of August 31.

“While [Tuesday]’s news is disappointing, Nurix remains in a strong position, with a substantial cash runway, three clinical-stage programs across our wholly owned and partnered portfolio, and an exciting preclinical pipeline,” Arthur T. Sands, MD, PhD, Nurix president and CEO, stated Tuesday after the close of markets.

sum: Roche closed recruitment this week for the Phase III ENVISION trial of Elevidys in older ambulatory and non-ambulatory Duchenne patients, a study that enrolled 90 participants across 14 countries. The company and partner Sarepta Therapeutics are now analyzing data from the first part of the trial. It is one of several pipeline and regulatory developments that have landed in quick succession — and that together frame the central question facing investors: how much of this progress is already reflected in the share price?

UBS delivered its verdict on Monday, cutting its rating on the Swiss drugmaker from "Buy" to "Neutral" while simultaneously lifting its price target to CHF 420 from CHF 376. According to media reports, the bank pointed to valuation following the stock's recent rally as the reason for the more cautious stance. Its medium-term thesis on Giredestrant, notably, remained intact — a combination that captures the tension neatly: a positive view of a drug candidate can coexist with a reserved view of the equity if the market has already priced in the expected progress.

That tension has real weight, because Roche shares have climbed 20% since the start of the year. The advance makes the valuation debate especially pertinent for anyone considering a fresh position, even if it does not by itself settle the stock's appeal.

The pipeline news flow has been broad. On Monday the FDA granted 510(k) clearance to the cobas eplex Respiratory Pathogen Panel 3, a test that Roche says can detect up to 19 viruses and bacteria from a single sample in the US. That provides a concrete regulatory foundation; what matters next is the commercial execution built on top of it.

Two further diagnostic milestones followed. On 27 October the cobas smart e immunoassay analyzer received CE marking, and a day later Roche announced the global launch of the VENTANA BAP1 (SP527) test, which supports the diagnosis of mesotheliomas and helps distinguish them from other tumors. For the analyzer, Roche is planning a test menu exceeding 100 assays — the rollout of that menu now becomes a tangible yardstick for how the CE mark translates into a broader offering.

BioNTech Spends $463 Million on Its Own Shares While Roche Picks Up the R&D Tab
sum: BioNTech has been putting its cash to work in more ways than one. By September 30, the company had repurchased 5,037,452 ADSs for a total of $463.3 million, according to its quarterly statement — a figure it booked as EUR 403.5 million. The buyback authority, approved for up to EUR 1.0 billion, runs until May 6, 2027.

The repurchase disclosure landed alongside a contractual shift in the company's collaboration with Roche/Genentech. BioNTech has exercised an option under which future research and development costs for the program will fall to Roche/Genentech from January 1, 2027. BioNTech retains the right to royalties should the program reach successful development and commercialization.

The third quarter of 2026 brought revenue of EUR 1,289.2 million, down from EUR 1,518.9 million in the same period a year earlier. Management pinned the decline on softer demand for COVID-19 vaccines. Net profit for the quarter came in at EUR 184.5 million — yet the year-to-date picture is far less flattering, with a net loss of EUR 1,168.2 million accumulated since January.

Against that backdrop, the balance sheet remains the company's loudest argument. Liquid funds and securities investments stood at EUR 16.2 billion at the end of the third quarter, while adjusted research and development costs for the same period amounted to EUR 578.5 million. That cushion gives BioNTech room to absorb both its R&D bill and the fading vaccine business — provided the money is channeled into programs that can eventually stand on their own.

BioNTech raised the lower bound of its 2026 revenue forecast, narrowing the expected range to EUR 1.7 billion to EUR 1.9 billion. The previous guidance had been EUR 1.6 billion to EUR 1.9 billion. The revision lifts both the floor and the midpoint of management's expectations — a positive shift, though a forecast is only an expectation until it is delivered.

Analysts, meanwhile, are recalibrating. Evercore ISI cut its price target to $110 from $120 on Wednesday while keeping its positive rating, according to media reports. The combination — confidence in the outlook paired with lower valuation expectations — reads as cautiously constructive rather than a vote of no confidence.

BioNTech Hands Roche the Bill While Its Own Trial Data Refuse to Cooperate
sum: BioNTech's investors got two very different kinds of news this week, and the gap between them says a lot about how the company should be valued. One item is a contract that shifts future spending onto a partner. The others are clinical readouts that, on close inspection, deliver less than the headlines might suggest.

Start with the money. Under a cost-sharing arrangement announced Tuesday for the joint program with Roche and Genentech, future research and development expenses are to be assigned in principle to Roche/Genentech from January 1, 2027. BioNTech would retain the right to royalties should development and commercialization succeed. The relief on the cost line is real, but so is the qualifier "in principle" — it does not mean BioNTech has shed every expense or every risk, and potential royalties are not revenue until the underlying conditions are met.

The financial backdrop is sturdier than the pipeline news. BioNTech reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of EUR 1,289.2 million and adjusted diluted earnings per share of EUR 1.76. Sales fell year on year, chiefly on weaker demand for COVID-19 vaccines. The company lifted its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to EUR 1.7 billion to EUR 1.9 billion, up from a prior range of EUR 1.6 billion to EUR 1.9 billion. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities stood at EUR 16.2 billion. Shares rose 3.9% the day after the quarterly figures and the raised outlook.
That cash cushion and the Roche handoff both buy time. Neither answers the question that actually moves the stock: whether the pipeline produces something worth paying for.

The clearest test case came on October 26, when BioNTech and DualityBio reported that the Phase 3 DYNASTY-Breast02 trial of trastuzumab pamirtecan hit its primary endpoint in metastatic HR+/HER2-low breast cancer. Progression-free survival improved versus investigator's choice of chemotherapy — statistically significant, but only moderately so.

The companies themselves capped the enthusiasm. Available efficacy and safety data suggested the potential patient benefit in this treatment landscape could be limited, and overall survival data were not yet mature. Next steps are under discussion.

items.t: Nurix Shares Drop 35% After Sanofi Scraps Oral Immunology Drug
sum: Nurix Therapeutics, Inc. (NRIX) lost roughly a third of its market value in extended trading Tuesday after Sanofi said it is walking away from an experimental oral drug licensed from the clinical-stage biotech.

The Paris-based pharmaceutical giant told Nurix it will halt the Phase 1 first-in-human study of SAR448272 and shut down the program altogether. The compound, an oral STAT6 degrader, was being tested for type 2 inflammatory and autoimmune conditions including atopic dermatitis and asthma. Shares of the San Francisco-based company fell 34% to 35% after the closing bell.

The termination strips Nurix of the milestone and royalty stream tied to that single asset. Under the 2019 collaboration, the company had been eligible for about $455 million in additional development, regulatory and commercial milestones on SAR448272, plus royalties on any future sales. Nurix has collected roughly $139 million from Sanofi under the partnership to date, including $10 million paid when the French drugmaker began early-stage testing of the compound earlier this year.
Nurix said it still stands to earn milestones and royalties on other programs licensed under the same alliance, provided Sanofi elects to push them forward.

"While today's news is disappointing, Nurix remains in a strong position, with a substantial cash runway, three clinical-stage programs across our wholly owned and partnered portfolio, and an exciting preclinical pipeline," Chief Executive Arthur T. Sands said.

The company said the setback does not change its cash runway guidance. As of August 31, Nurix held $1.1 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, which it expects to fund operations into the second half of 2029.
Nurix has no approved products, so its revenue comes almost entirely from collaboration payments. Besides Sanofi, it has partnerships with Roche, Gilead and Pfizer.

Jess McClain’s Coach Shares a Long-Run Tweak for Fatigue Resistance
sum: Many runners think of the climbs as the toughest part of a hilly race. Uphills send your heart rate soaring and slow even the strongest runners to a grind, while descents offer a chance to catch your breath and let gravity do some of the work. But David Roche, ultramarathoner and coach to New York City Marathon women’s runner-up Jess McClain, says those easier-feeling downhills can come at a cost later in the race.
And Roche knows the importance of late-race performance, which is why he integrates strategies into his training to fight fatigue through long distances.

Take McClain’s finish in New York City as an example: She outkicked reigning champ Hellen Obiri just feet from the finish line to take second place by mere seconds, clocking 2:24:42 and becoming the first American woman to reach the podium in NYC since 2018.

Roche’s fatigue-fighting tactics take him even farther in his own races. The two-time Life Time Leadville 100 winner—and course record holder—covered the famously demanding trails in 15:12:30, averaging roughly 9:07 per mile. Yet he rarely relies on extremely long, arduous training runs to prepare for conquering late miles.

Instead, Roche uses downhill workouts to reproduce some of the muscular stress that can cause runners’ legs to fail in an endurance event. “Downhills are the gateway to fatigue resistance in these really long events,” Roche tells Runner’s World.

The best part is, you don’t have to be an elite like McClain or Roche to benefit from his advice. He shares how purposeful downhill training can help runners preserve their strength, form, and pace deep into a race. Plus, he offers his go-to workout to add to your buildup.

Running downhill may provide some relief to your cardiovascular system—by lowering your heart rate a bit as gravity naturally carries you downward—but it puts much more strain on your musculoskeletal system. To keep you from tumbling down the hill, the quads must repeatedly brake the body’s momentum.
